opus-5.5.text:
I think it's important to separate what "open" actually means here, because there's a lot of confusion. When a lab releases weights, they're giving you the final artifact, the compiled binary, essentially. You can run it, fine-tune it, deploy it. That's genuinely valuable, and I don't want to dismiss it. But you can't really reproduce it. You don't know what data went in, how it was filtered, what the training recipe was, what decisions were made along the way about what the model should or shouldn't do.

From the developer's side, I understand the logic. The weights are, in some sense, the least defensible part of the business. Once a model is out there, a competitor will match it in six months anyway. Releasing weights builds an ecosystem, gets developers using your architecture, your tokenizer, your tooling, and it buys a lot of goodwill. Meanwhile the real competitive advantage, the data pipelines, the curation, the infrastructure, the know-how of actually training at scale, stays in-house. There are also legal reasons. A lot of training data has unclear licensing, and publishing exactly what you trained on invites lawsuits. And some people will make a safety argument, though I find that one a bit inconsistent, since the weights are the part that actually carries the capability.

The issue for me is trust. If these models become the interface through which people access information, make decisions, interact with services, then you need to be able to verify what's inside them. With open weights alone, you can't audit for backdoors, you can't check for biases baked in through data selection, you can't really know whose interests the model serves. It's like being handed a binary and told it's open source.

That's why I think the long-term answer has to be something closer to fully open, open data, open training code, ideally verifiable training, where you can actually prove that a given set of weights came from a given process. And I think that also requires rethinking the economics, so the people contributing data and compute are actually rewarded, rather than everything being concentrated in a few companies who decide what to share and what to hold back. Open weights are a good step, but they're a step, not the destination.

r001.rationale: The response says developers keep data pipelines, curation, infrastructure, and training know-how in-house as competitive advantages, but it does not clearly identify preserving monetization opportunities as the reason for withholding source code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think you have to separate what people mean by "open" here, because the term has been stretched a lot. When a lab releases weights, what you actually get is the artifact — the final output of a very expensive process. You can run it, you can fine-tune it, you can build on top of it. That's genuinely useful, and I don't want to dismiss it. But it's closer to getting a compiled binary than getting source code.

The real "source" of a model is the data, the data pipeline, the filtering decisions, the training recipe, the hyperparameters, the infrastructure code, the evals you ran along the way. And that's exactly the part that's being held back. From the lab's perspective it's pretty rational. The weights are a snapshot — in six months they're going to be obsolete anyway. But the pipeline is the thing that lets you produce the next model, and the one after that. That's where the competitive moat is, and also where the legal exposure is, because the moment you publish your data mix, people can go line by line and ask where everything came from.

So there's a business reason and a liability reason, and both push the same direction: open the weights, keep the recipe.

The problem I have with it is what it does to the ecosystem. If only the artifact is open, you can't actually reproduce it, you can't verify what went into it, and you can't meaningfully audit it. You're trusting the lab's description of what the model is. And more practically, it means the community can't learn from the process. Every group that wants to train something has to rediscover the same things from scratch. We did a lot of this with the original transformer work — the fact that the paper and the code were out there is what let the whole field iterate on it. If attention had been released as a frozen checkpoint with no description of how it was trained, I don't think we get the same explosion of progress.

So I'd say: open weights is a step, and I'm glad it exists, because the alternative where everything sits behind an API is worse. But I'd push back on calling it open source. Open source, to me, means someone else can take what you published and rebuild it, change it, and understand it. Weights alone don't give you that. And I think the labs that eventually go the full distance — data, code, recipe, all of it — are the ones that will actually get a community building with them rather than just consuming from them.

r001.rationale: The response cites business reasons and preserving a competitive moat, but does not clearly say that withholding source code is meant to preserve monetization opportunities.

astra-6.text:
I think there are different levels of openness here. If you release the weights, people can run the model, fine-tune it, and build applications without depending on your API. That’s meaningful. But it doesn’t necessarily let them reproduce how you got there.

The training code, the data preparation, the decisions you made along the way—that’s a lot of the knowledge behind the model. A developer might want the adoption that comes from releasing weights while keeping some of that knowledge as a competitive advantage. There could also be practical constraints around releasing the code or data, so I wouldn’t assume there’s one motivation.

For me, the useful question is: what does this release allow other people to do? Using a model, studying it, and reproducing it are different capabilities. Calling all of them “open” can obscure those differences.

r001.rationale: The response says developers may release weights for adoption while keeping training knowledge as a competitive advantage, but it does not clearly connect withholding source code to preserving monetization opportunities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are different levels of openness here. If you release the weights, people can run the model, fine-tune it, and build something on top of it. That’s useful. But it doesn’t necessarily let them reproduce how you got there. For that, you need the training code, the data, and the process around it.

From the developer’s perspective, that can be a strategic choice. You want people using your model and building an ecosystem around it, while keeping some advantage in how you train the next one. So you’re opening the artifact, but holding back part of the recipe.

The question is what we want openness to enable. If it’s deployment and experimentation, weights get you pretty far. If it’s reproducibility and the ability for others to independently improve the whole process, weights alone aren’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response says developers may keep a training advantage while encouraging model use and ecosystem growth, but it does not clearly connect withholding source code to preserving monetization opportunities.
